paras: The threatened lynching of John Wilson took place at Valparaiso, Indiana, in August 1903, when armed white farmers pursued a Black man accused of attacking a farmer's wife and then crowded the town's streets threatening to lynch him at the county jail. The sheriff guarded the jail, no attack was made, and Wilson was later sentenced to two to fourteen years in prison. The wire carried the story under headlines such as 'Indiana Farmers Thirst for Blood', and the hostility it stirred drove some Black residents from the town.

According to the Indianapolis Journal, on the afternoon of Saturday, August 8, a Black stranger asked for matches at a Washington township farmhouse where a farmer's wife was alone with two small children. Returning to ask for salt and pepper, he was said to have choked and kicked her while attempting to 'criminally assault' her, until the children's cries frightened him away. The wire named her Mrs. Hugh F. Bitt or Bitts; the Journal's local dispatches called her Mrs. U. S. Biggs.

Relatives and neighbors armed with shotguns formed a posse of 'nearly 100', but the fugitive escaped on a passing freight train. Neighbors said that had the posse caught him first, 'they would have made quick work of him.' Deputy Sheriff Matthews and William Wilson, a school teacher, met the train at Warsaw in the wire version or Wanatah in the Journal's. By the captors' account the man drew a knife, and William Wilson felled him with a stone.

Bound and gagged, he was jailed at Valparaiso that evening and gave his name as John Wilson of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania. Within an hour, the Plymouth Tribune said, angry farmers of Washington township crowded the streets 'bent upon dealing summary punishment' to him. Farmers bought cartridges and a business man offered rope, but 'the crowd lacked a leader', and the sheriff doubled his armed guard. New York papers said the crowds, joined by college students, threatened to break the jail on Sunday as well.

On the night of August 10, with armed guards still at the jail, a rumor that Wilson would be moved to Michigan City brought armed farmers, friends of the Biggs family, to wait along the roadside for a chance to take him.

Pastors and prominent citizens urged that the law take its course. The authorities, the Journal said, publicly understated the woman's injuries so that neighbors' feeling would subside. The 'incensed feeling' caused a number of Black residents to leave for Chicago, and two Black businessmen were 'practically forced to suspend.'
A week later A. J. Bowser, editor of the Chesterton Tribune, began organized opposition to Black settlement in Porter County, warning that 'lynchings would follow' it.

On August 22 Wilson was quietly taken from jail for a preliminary hearing, because 'the bitter feeling against Wilson has not died yet', and was bound over under $5,000. On October 6 Judge Tuthill of the Porter Superior Court heard a dozen witnesses and sentenced him to two to fourteen years at Michigan City; Wilson had contended that another Black man committed the act.

The wire story ran on August 9 and 10 from Wichita and Louisville to Arizona, Birmingham and Atlanta. It called Wilson 'a powerful negro' and stated his guilt and confession as fact, under headlines such as 'Food for Lynchers', 'Indiana Farmers Thirst for Blood' and 'Indiana Mob After Black Brutes'. Two papers printed it beneath a Hattiesburg, Mississippi, lynching of the same night.

The Indianapolis Journal's own correspondent followed the case for two months, treating the assault as proven while crediting the sheriff's 'determined stand'. The Plymouth Tribune headed its account 'Threatened Lynching at Valparaiso' and closed that 'better counsel prevailed.' The New York Sun and Tribune took up the case mainly as the occasion for Bowser's campaign, under 'Wants No More Negroes' and 'Wants Blacks Kept Out'. The Journal ran the same campaign as 'Bold Editor's Views', noting that Wilson had 'narrowly escaped lynching'; no Black-press report of the episode was found.
Beyond names and places, accounts of a confession differed: the wire said he confessed, the Journal that he admitted assault and battery but denied rape.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Wilson
bases: Crowds of armed farmers threatened to lynch a jailed Black man accused of attacking a white farmer's wife (A12, A17), an armed posse had pursued him (A2), and armed farmers later waited on the roadside to take him if he were moved (A10); no attack on the jail was made, so this is a threatened lynching.
The wire report (A1), the Indianapolis Journal's own specials (A2, A8, A10) and the Plymouth Tribune (A12) independently describe the pursuit, the capture and the threatening crowds at Valparaiso.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A 'powerful negro' attempted to assault a farmer's wife, fled by freight to Warsaw, attacked a deputy with a knife, was knocked unconscious and 'confessed'; angry farmers filled the streets 'muttering threats of vengeance' but no jail attack was feared.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal specials
accounts.gist: Fuller local version: a posse of nearly 100 with shotguns, capture at Wanatah, admission of assault and battery but denial of rape, and lynching talk that failed because 'the crowd lacked a leader'; later the roadside wait and Black departures.

accounts.label: Arresting officers' account
accounts.gist: Wilson drew a knife and attacked or threatened Matthews before William Wilson felled him with a stone; this comes only from the arresting side.

accounts.label: Wilson's defense
accounts.gist: He pleaded not guilty and contended that another Black man committed the act.

accounts.label: Laporte dispatches (New York papers)
accounts.gist: Crowds of farmers and college or Normal School students filled the streets on Sunday threatening to break the jail; the case prompted Bowser's movement against Black settlement.

framing.detail: The wire story ran under headlines such as 'Food for Lynchers', 'Indiana Farmers Thirst for Blood' and 'Indiana Mob After Black Brutes', calling Wilson 'a powerful negro' and stating his guilt and confession as fact.

The Indianapolis Journal treated the assault as proven ('the negro John Wilson, who assaulted Mrs. U. S. Biggs') while praising the sheriff's 'determined stand' and reporting citizens' gratitude that no mob violence occurred.
The Plymouth Tribune headed its story 'Threatened Lynching at Valparaiso' and closed that 'better counsel prevailed and the law will be allowed to take its course.'

The Sun, the New-York Tribune and the Journal reported Bowser's campaign ('Wants No More Negroes', 'Bold Editor's Views') and quoted his warning that 'lynchings would follow' Black settlement without comment.

info: Assault and pursuit on the afternoon of Saturday, Aug. 8, 1903, with crowds in the streets that night; A21 dates the assault Aug. 7.
A farm in Washington township near Valparaiso; capture at Wanatah (A2) or Warsaw (A1, A12); threats in the streets of Valparaiso around the county jail.
John Wilson, a Black man who said he was from Pittsburg, Pa., and had worked on the railroad
Accused of choking and kicking a white farmer's wife (Mrs. U. S. Biggs; 'Mrs. Hugh F. Bitt(s)' in the wire) while attempting to 'criminally assault' her
Relatives, neighbors and farmers of Washington township; New York reports add college or Normal School students in the street crowds
Sentenced by Judge Tuthill to two to fourteen years in the state prison at Michigan City and a $10 fine (A21); A22 says fourteen years
